title: Introduction
text:
4.1 Ecosystem representation
Incorporating ecosystem types in the SCP process serves to broadly capture the spatial distribution of distinct-biological communities, and thereby the full suite of species—i.e., gamma diversity (Whittaker 1960)—across the region of interest (Mucina 2024). Following the previous terrestrial SCP for KwaZulu-Natal (Escott 2010), a vegetation-type map formed a robust surrogate for ecosystem types. Vegetation types commonly serve as surrogates for ecosystem types because they largely capture differences in biodiversity patterns across the landscape (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024).
For an up-to-date representation of ecosystem extent, the provincial-vegetation map (i.e., coverage) had to be adjusted. The provincial-vegetation coverage serves as a representation of “natural” vegetation communities prior to GC pressures ca. 1750 (Mucina et al. 2018). Therefore, the coverage had to be adjusted to reflect the current state of ecosystems using the best available data.

Figure 1: Overview of the landscape integrity evaluation to idenifying landscape corridors. 1. A modification coverage is used to identify natural, near-natural, and functional areas. 2. By applying a resistance surface of species movement through the modified landscape, 3. a fragmentation analysis can be performed, to 4. identify corridors for species movement, and areas with good landscape integritiy, i.e., high connectivity, sufficient number and size of habitat patches. R Core Team (2025) packages ‘landscapemetrics’ (Hesselbarth et al. 2019) was used to analyse landscape integrity, and ‘gdistance’ (van Etten 2017) to estimate least-cost paths, and ‘grainscape’ (Chubaty et al. 2025) to evaluate graph connectivity.

title: Priotitization analyses
text:
To find the best working solution to the KZN Conservation Plan the R Core Team (2025) prioritizr package (Hanson et al. 2025) was used. There are a number of advantages to this approach. Unlike simulated annealing (e.g., Marxan), where near-optimal solutions are obtained through multiple runs, prioritizr uses mixed-integer linear programming, in a single run, to solve for the optimal solution. The formulation how ‘cost’ is balanced across a landscape to delineate space for biodiversity (or other) features, that is, the ‘conservation problem’, is highly customisable using the prioritizr framework. As such, planners can explicitly control many conservation-problem parameters. Running a single run, versus multiple, to find the optimal solution speeds up complex problem solving substantially.
Some of this complexity in solving prioritizr conservation problems includes advanced methods for zoning, and tuning landscape connectivity and patch size (Hanson et al. 2025). The prioritizr package integrates with R Core Team (2025) GIS environments enabling open source data pipeline development for conservation planning.
Prioritizr has had a broad uptake and is helping solve conservation problems; some interesting examples include:

European terrestrial realm priority areas for 10‒30% protection scenarios (Visconti et al. 2024),
National government marine biodiversity in Mozambique (Jones et al. 2021),
Freshwater catchment and biodiversity conservation in Canada (Southee et al. 2021),
Marine genetic diversity (and socio-economic scenarios) in South Africa (West Coast) (Nielsen et al. 2023),
Climate resilience on South Africa’s West Coast (Nielsen et al. 2023),
Functional and taxonomic diversity conservation planning in China’s terrestrial realm (national) (Liu et al. 2026), and
Restoration in the Brazilian Cerrado (Aragõ et al. 2026).


pkgs <- c("prioritizr")
to_install <- pkgs[!pkgs %in% installed.packages()[, "Package"]]
if (length(to_install) > 0) install.packages(to_install)

lapply(pkgs, library, character.only = TRUE)

[[1]]

[6] "datasets"   "methods"    "base"      




The ‘conservation problem’ in prioritizr is resolved as a function of the following (Hanson et al. 2025),
\[problem = f(objectives + targets + constraints + penalties),\]
where

objectives are the overall goals of the conservation planning exercise.

Conventionally, the ‘min set’ objective is aimed for whereby enough habitat for all species is sought at minimum cost.
Custom objectives can be set and compared.

targets set the minimum proportion or amount of each feature’s spatial distribution that should ideally be protected.
constraints forbid solutions that either exhibit or do not exhibit a particular characteristic.

For example, ‘lock in’ or ‘lock out’ specific planning units to a zone, e.g., ‘irreplaceable’.
The contiguity of planning units can also be set to determine connectivity and patch size trade-offs. This can be achieved per feature.
Planning units can be constrained to a particular zone, e.g., restoration, or low utilisation.

penalties function to limit or penalize solutions that do not meet a specific characteristic.

For example, favour clumping to produce contiguous areas, or
reduce spatial fragmentation.

title: Introduction
text:
1.1 The Plan objective
This terrestrial conservation plan aims to solve the problem of ensuring space for biodiversity conservation, in the KwaZulu-Natal terrestrial realm, whilst minimising cost. This solution is also known as the minimum set of protected areas solution (i.e., the ‘min set’) (Margules and Pressey 2000; Hanson et al. 2025). In order to provide a robust solution to this problem three broad requirements need to be fulfilled (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024; Jung et al. 2025).
We need to know:

What biodiversity and where is it?
What is the state of this biodiversity?
Where and how should conservation efforts be prioritised?

The first question involves the collation and modelling of data to provide the best possible spatial representation of biodiversity. This approach helps guarantee that conservation efforts are directed to the most appropriate locations. The second question concerns the conservation or risk status of biodiversity. This information is drawn from national and regional biodiversity assessments and offers guidance on which species should receive attention in our planning exercises. The third question will guide the mapping of biodiversity and the prioritisation analyses described in point three.

title: Priotitization analyses
text:
To find the best working solution to the KZN Conservation Plan the R Core Team (2025) prioritizR package (Hanson et al. 2025) was used. There are a number of advantages to this approach. Unlike simulated annealing (e.g., Marxan), where near-optimal solutions are obtained through multiple runs, prioritizR uses mixed-integer linear programming, in a single run, to solve for the optimal solution (Note 1). The formulation how ‘cost’ is balanced across a landscape to delineate space for biodiversity (or other) features, that is, the ‘conservation problem’, is highly customisable using the prioritizr framework. As such, planners can explicitly control many conservation-problem parameters. Running a single run, versus multiple, to find the optimal solution speeds up complex problem-solving substantially.








Note 1: PrioritiR–Marxan integration



PrioritizR was set up to compare and run Marxan simulations. For a Marxan run prioritizR will accept Marxan formatted data and perform a Marxan run simulation. This means that preparation of data for prioritizR can be the same as for a Marxan run making integration, comparison, and movement between these planning tools seamless.


Some of this complexity in prioritizR conservation-problem solving includes advanced methods for zoning, and landscape connectivity and patch size (Hanson et al. 2025). The prioritizR package integrates with R Core Team (2025) GIS environments enabling open source data pipeline development for conservation planning.
PrioritizR has had a broad uptake and is helping solve conservation problems; some interesting examples include:

European terrestrial realm priority areas for 10‒30% protection scenarios (Visconti et al. 2024),
National government marine biodiversity in Mozambique (Jones et al. 2021),
Freshwater catchment and biodiversity conservation in Canada (Southee et al. 2021),
Marine genetic diversity (and socio-economic scenarios) in South Africa (West Coast) (Nielsen et al. 2023),
Climate resilience on South Africa’s West Coast (Nielsen et al. 2023),
Functional and taxonomic diversity conservation planning in China’s terrestrial realm (national) (Liu et al. 2026), and
Restoration in the Brazilian Cerrado (Aragõ et al. 2026).



The ‘conservation problem’ in prioritizr is resolved as a function of the following (Hanson et al. 2025),
\[problem = f(objectives + targets + constraints + penalties),\]
where

objectives are the overall goals of the conservation planning exercise.

Conventionally, the ‘min set’ objective is aimed for whereby enough habitat for all species is sought at minimum cost.
Custom objectives can be set and compared.

targets set the minimum proportion or amount of each feature’s spatial distribution that should ideally be protected.
constraints forbid solutions that either exhibit or do not exhibit a particular characteristic.

For example, ‘lock in’ or ‘lock out’ specific planning units to a zone, e.g., ‘irreplaceable’.
The contiguity of planning units can also be set to determine connectivity and patch size trade-offs. This can be achieved per feature.
Planning units can be constrained to a particular zone, e.g., restoration, or low utilisation.

penalties function to limit or penalize solutions that do not meet a specific characteristic.

For example, favour clumping to produce contiguous areas, or
reduce spatial fragmentation.

There are three broad stages towards the resolution of this problem (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024; Jung et al. 2025):

What biodiversity and where is it?
What space does this biodiversity need?
Where and how should conservation efforts be prioritised?

The first question involves the collation and modelling of data to provide the best possible spatial representation of biodiversity. This approach helps guarantee that conservation efforts are directed to the most appropriate locations. The second question concerns the conservation or risk status of biodiversity. This information is drawn from national and regional biodiversity assessments and offers guidance on which species should receive attention in our planning exercises. The third question will guide the mapping of biodiversity and the prioritisation analyses described in point three.

title: Introduction
text:
1.1 Plan aim & stages
This terrestrial conservation plan aims to solve the problem of: how to ensure sufficient space for biodiversity conservation, in the KwaZulu-Natal terrestrial realm, whilst simultaneously minimising constraints and maximising opportunities (see Note 2). This is also known as the minimum set of protected areas’ solution (i.e., the ‘min set’) (Margules and Pressey 2000; Hanson et al. 2025). There are four broad stages that need to be addressed for resolution of this conservation problem (Escott et al. 2016; SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024) (Figure 1).








Note 1: Costs & decision support



Constraints and opportunities are referred as costs in conservation planning. These costs are more than the monetary value of acquiring protected areas for conservation efforts. In conservation planning ‘costing’ involves how complex socio-ecological factors are quantified and tradeoffs made. The balancing of these tradeoffs is the ‘decision support’ mechanism that helps optimise the conservation planning solution with other human land use activities (Escott et al. 2016; SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024).

Figure 1: The iterative stages, from gathering data, target setting, to prioritisation analyses, in conservation planning (c.f. SANBI and UNEP-WCMC (2024)). (1) The first stage addresses the what and where of biodiversity-related landscape features. (2) The second speaks to goal setting for the space biodiversity needs. (3) The third stage deals with setting up decision-making criteria that helps balance tradeoffs between the ‘costs’ of conservation efforts and socio-ecological factors (see Note 2). (4) Finally, the forth involves a robust and transparent analysis that solves the problem of the where and how should conservation efforts be prioritised at minimum ‘cost’.



The what and where of biodiversity-related features requires a collation and modelling of biodiversity occurrence data in order to provide the best possible spatial representation of biodiversity. This helps guarantee that conservation efforts are directed to the most appropriate locations. Other important what and where features for biodiversity include key habitat features for breeding, or safe zones (refugia).
The second stage concerns determination of meaningful representation and persistence targets. In other words, how much of which ecosystems and ecological features need to be represented, in the conservation plan, to secure the persistence of biodiversity. Setting up decision-support mechanisms helps us ensure that conservation efforts are focused on optimal locations. For this, other land uses and socio-ecological dynamics have to be considered (Margules and Pressey 2000; Hanson et al. 2025). Once this data is gathered the final stage involves the prioritisation analysis. Multiple analyses are run showing different scenarios in a transparent process to demonstrate how the plan attempts to optimise conservation while supporting critical socio-ecological dynamics (Escott et al. 2016; SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024).

title: Introduction
text:
1.2 Integration with the biodiversity realms
Ensuring integration of this terrestrial realm conservation plan, with the marine, estuarine, and freshwater biodiversity realms is critical for a connected land- to sea-scape approach. Integration ensures that critical marine realms are supported by important estuaries. These estuaries are supported by a freshwater plan, and conservation in linked terrestrial environs is prioritised to promote this overall land–ocean ‘scape’ ― a multi-realm ‘ecoscape’ (Wedding et al. 2025).
The above linking from marine, estuary, freshwater to terrestrial, describes the hierarchical approach recommended for integrating biodiversity plans (Escott et al. 2016; Lötter 2015). This ‘linking’ is done from the most dependant, that is, most affected by other adjacent realms, to the least dependent realm. The terrestrial realm is considered the ‘least’ dependent, compared with the marine and estuarine realms, in KwaZulu-Natal (Escott et al. 2016).








Note 2: Terrestrial and freshwater overlap



Wetlands provide an interesting case of overlap in the terrestrial and freshwater realms. Many species directly use both of ‘realms’. The terrestrial plan accounts for this overlap through its incorporation freshwater features, that is, ‘freshwater’ associated species, and freshwater bodies (Escott et al. 2016; Lötter 2015). The terrestrial plan is however specifically engineered to address terrestrial-focused conservation problems necessitating a separate exercise to address freshwater conservation planning.


Overlap between realms has to be dealt with systematically. For conservation planning in KwaZulu-Natal, the rugged topography with incised valleys and associated catchment systems is best addressed through a catchment management approach (Escott et al. 2016; Desmet and Hawley 2019). This catchment management system neatly ties the terrestrial to the estuarine, coastal and marine realms.
The stages1 of this SCP are as follows:

The what and where of biodiversity — feature representation (see ATsec-eco-state):

Develop a baseline‑ecosystem layer that broadly represents the spatial distribution of biotic communities (i.e., coarse‑filter features).
Determine the state of ecosystems and their biodiversity:

Ascertain the distribution of protected and conserved areas.
Refine the baseline‑ecosystems layer to represent the current state of biodiversity.

Bolster the representation of all species.2
Represent ecosystem function and change — collection of additional spatial datasets.3

Ecosystem processes

Ecosystem infrastructure

Ecosystem services

Ecological condition

Climate change information

Socio‑economic data


Determine the current state of ecosystems and their biodiversity:

Evaluate the risk and protection status of ecosystems.
Align and compare provincial (and where appropriate trans‑regional) ecosystem risk status.
Evaluate the risk and protection status of species.

Set representation and persistence targets:

Representation and persistence of ecosystems, including alignment with the Global Biodiversity Framework (Convention on Biological Diversity 2022).
Representation and persistence of species.

Spatial prioritisation:

Spatial framework of evaluation — planning units.
Compilation of cost (decision‑support) layers.
Systematic spatial prioritisation analyses and scenario modelling.
Sensitivity analysis.

Product development.

title: Ecosystem representation
text:
Incorporating ecosystem types in the conservation planning process serves to broadly capture the spatial distribution of distinct-biological communities, and associated species diversity, that is, the gamma diversity (Whittaker 1960)across the region of interest (Mucina 2024). Following the previous terrestrial SCP for KwaZulu-Natal (Escott 2010), a vegetation-type map formed a robust surrogate for ecosystem types. Vegetation types commonly serve as surrogates for ecosystem types because they largely capture differences in biodiversity patterns across the landscape (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024).
For an up-to-date representation of ecosystem extent, the provincial-vegetation map (i.e., coverage) had to be adjusted. The provincial-vegetation coverage serves as a representation of “natural” vegetation communities prior to GC pressures ca. 1750 (Mucina et al. 2018). Therefore, the coverage had to be adjusted to reflect the current state of ecosystems using the best available data.

title: Features overview ― the what and where of biodiversity
text:
1 The what and where of biodiversity
For robust representation of biodiversity, and associated ecosystem infrastructure and services into the future, the what and where of biodiversity has to be considered. Moreover, the functions of biodiversity, and associated ecosystems, also need to be considered for accurate representation when attempting to ensure conservation of these features.
In order to maximise representation of biodiversity in a landscape, the conservation planning process adopts a two-pronged approach, specifically:

a wide-ranging (or coarse-filter): “Ecosystem representation” approach (see Ecosystems), and

a targeted (or fine-filter): “Species representation” approach (see section Species) (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024).

Representation of the ecosystem types in the area-of-interest largely fulfils the wide-ranging component, that is, if the SCP incorporates the full diversity of ecosystems, it is likely to represent their constituent taxa. The complementary approach, that is, the targeted approach, caters for specific, threatened taxa, or those not operating within the parameters of represented ecosystems (Margules and Pressey 2000).






References

Margules, Christopher Robert, and Robert L Pressey. 2000. “Systematic Conservation Planning.” Nature 405 (6783): 243–53.


SANBI, and UNEP-WCMC. 2024. Mapping Biodiversity Priorities: A Practical Approach to Spatial Biodiversity Assessment and Priortisation to Inform National Policy, Planning, Decisions and Action. 2nd ed. South African National Biodiversity Institute. Pretoria, ZA.

title: Species representation
text:
The broad-ranging ecosystem representation is complemented by a targeted approach that focuses on specific species (see ?@sec-spp-rep). The targeted approach required a systematic selection of species (SANBI and UNEP-WCMC 2024). Ezemvelo KZN Wildlife scientists and a broad range of stakeholders developed the criteria for the inclusion of species (Elliot 2023). For the KwaZulu-Natal conservation plan, these criteria were applied to each group of taxa: Amphibians, Aquatic taxa, Invertebrates, Mammals, Plants, and Reptiles.







Table 1: Criteria for inclusion of species in the targeted approach.
